key_insight: The paper turns short-range-order alloy design into a differentiable optimization problem, enabling direct gradient-based tuning from target SRO to target mechanical property.
engineering_relevance: This provides a faster, scalable route for property-driven design of high-entropy alloys, reducing reliance on costly random-swap searches and trial-and-error simulation loops.
method: Treat atom occupancy as continuous and optimize SRO with gradient descent instead of reverse Monte Carlo random swaps.
Add a physics-based correction term to keep generated multi-element structures thermodynamically realistic.
Use a small neural network to map composition and SRO statistics to mechanical properties, closing the inverse-design loop.
evidence_signal: Across nine FCC/BCC alloys, the pipeline reproduced SRO-driven stiffness shifts from -20% to +57%, was about 6x faster and 8x more accurate on 4000-atom systems, and matched 3 of 4 cobalt-chromium-nickel target stiffness values within 6%.
watch_item: Small simulation cells can mislead SRO-property trends, so the method needs sufficiently large systems (at least 864 atoms in this study) and careful thermodynamic regularization.
paper_title: Differentiable inverse design of short-range order in high-entropy alloys: from target sro to target property
